ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for konbini OTC is not shelf space, POS integration or the law. It is a supply of licensed humans awake at 3 a.m., speaking Vietnamese or Chinese, who can explain a drug in 90 seconds. Chains will assume they can build this in-house, but they lack pharmacist labor and multilingual night coverage. A neutral network that any owner can join in an afternoon has the advantage, because independent and multi-chain owners have no other option.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one licensed Osaka pharmacy, or set up the pharmacy entity, and recruit 10-15 remote pharmacists for night and weekend slots. Build the QR, video, certificate and clerk-verification flow as a web app, tested at my three stores on quasi-drugs and referral flow. Pre-sign letters of intent with 10 owners for spring 2027 pricing. Approach two hotels near Namba for guest access. Meet the health-center pharmacy inspection office to confirm the compliance path before launch.

ideas.title: Payment-Slip Doctor for Foreign Residents
ideas.one_liner: A LINE service that lets a foreign resident photograph a Japanese payment slip or government letter and get a plain explanation, deadline, consequences and payment help in their own language.
ideas.customer: Japanese-language schools, vocational schools and universities with many foreign students, at about ¥300 per student per month. Later customers are municipal national-health-insurance departments paying for improved collection, employers of foreign staff, and rent-guarantee and property-management firms.
ideas.problem: Foreign residents paid on average only 63% of national health insurance premiums by the end of 2024, according to a survey of about 150 local governments. From around FY2027, unpaid premiums and pension contributions will be a ground to deny visa renewal or change of status. Yet at my counter, foreign customers regularly hand me a slip or official letter and ask what it means. The barcode on a konbini payment slip is void after the due date, so I have to refuse it. Then a worker who cannot get to the ward office in daytime faces an arrears spiral that may end in a denied visa. The government mails a notice in Japanese that looks like junk mail.
ideas.solution: Photograph the slip or letter. The service reads the barcode and text, identifies the document type such as national health insurance, resident tax, pension or traffic fine, and explains in Vietnamese, Nepali, Chinese, Burmese or Indonesian what it is, how much, when due, and the consequences of non-payment. It sets calendar reminders and links to pay by PayPay, bank app or konbini. If the slip is expired, it generates a reissue script and shows ward-office hours and the nearest late-opening branch. Anything ambiguous or legal is escalated to a partner administrative scrivener. Stickers with a QR code at konbini payment counters are the acquisition channel.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 system upgrades that will link municipal payment records to Immigration Services Agency data, plus the rule that unpaid premiums will block renewals from around 2027, make payment compliance a visa issue for hundreds of thousands of students and workers. The current government has made foreign-resident rule enforcement a political priority. Schools are already adding payment-tracking features to their student systems. Nobody has built the explanation layer, and translation apps do not decode payment slips or their deadlines.
ideas.revenue_model: Schools pay ¥300-500 per student per month. Municipalities pay per successful on-time payment or a share of recovered arrears. Employers pay per foreign employee per month. Property managers and guarantors pay per tenant. A small paid human-escalation tier costs the user ¥980 per case.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The failure point is not language in general. It is a single document, the konbini payment slip, and a single hidden rule that its barcode dies on the due date. People miss it by a day and the consequence is a visa problem. The counter clerk sees this daily, so the demand is proven and concentrated. Because the buyer of the outcome is a school or municipality, the paying customer is not the end user.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the LINE OA with barcode decoding, OCR and slip-type rules for the five most common slips, and Vietnamese, Nepali and Chinese output reviewed by native speakers. Put QR stickers on the payment counters of my three stores. Pilot with two Osaka language schools, about 300 students, at ¥300 per student per month. Measure on-time payment before and after. Bring the results to one ward's national health insurance department. Partner with an administrative scrivener firm for the escalation tier.

ideas.title: Konbini Pulse: Owner-Run Launch Verdict Panel
ideas.one_liner: A paid panel of convenience-store owners who report real shelf sell-through of new items in the first 48 hours after each Tuesday launch, sold to food makers who otherwise see only HQ's verdict.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size food and beverage makers, including OEM and private-label suppliers and exclusive-item partners of the big three chains, at ¥150k-500k per brand per month. Later customers are ad agencies, trend and product-development teams, and investors who follow listed food companies.
ideas.problem: Every chain launches dozens to hundreds of new items on Tuesdays. An item's fate is effectively decided in 3-10 days, and HQ decides listing and delisting on its own data. The maker, who invested in a line, packaging and ingredients, sees only what HQ tells them. Owners see the real signal: stock-out times, leftover at closing, repeat buyers versus first-day curiosity, counter comments, and differences between office districts and residential areas. That information is never shared with the supplier. Makers cannot tell whether a delisting was fair, so they cannot negotiate.
ideas.solution: A 30-second phone routine for each owner: photograph the shelf at fixed times on days 1, 2 and 3, log leftover count at the disposal scan, and tap one of a few reasons customers gave. The panel of 40-150 stores across chains and neighborhoods is aggregated into a '48-hour verdict' delivered to the maker by Thursday: sell-through curve, sell-out time, leftover, repeat rate, and buyer profile by district type. It uses shelf observations and the owner's own counts, not HQ system exports, to reduce contractual risk. Owners are paid monthly, so the panel is a new income line that does not depend on royalty.
ideas.why_now: Ingredient and rice inflation has squeezed maker margins, so a failed launch is more expensive than before. SKU churn is accelerating. Japan's revised subcontract law, in force since January 2026, tightens buyers' duty to negotiate prices with commissioned manufacturers, so evidence has value in negotiations. Alternative-data buyers and product teams have no view into konbini shelves, because chain POS data is proprietary.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription per brand, ¥150k-500k a month, plus ¥50k per launch report for smaller makers. Custom studies and delisting-defense reports cost ¥300k-1M. Owners receive ¥8-15k a month in cash plus a revenue share. Aggregate trend data is licensed to agencies and investors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Suppliers are structurally blind because the only party that counts their sales is the party that decides their fate. The owners standing at the shelf are the only independent observers, and they are invisible to the market because no one pays them. Once owners are paid to observe, the supplier's negotiating position changes. The moat is a trusted network of owners, not software. Data that comes from a shelf photo and a leftover count is less exposed to franchise confidentiality clauses than POS exports.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 12 stores across the three chains in Osaka through owner chat groups and the franchisee union, paying ¥10k a month each. Build a phone app that takes shelf photos on a schedule and captures counts in a few taps. Choose the next Tuesday launch wave and produce one '48-hour verdict' for five Osaka-area makers with konbini exclusives, offered at ¥50k per launch. Get legal review of the franchise contract clauses on data before scaling. Convert three makers to monthly subscriptions by day 90.

ideas.title: Gate-Risk Radar for Evergreen Private Credit
ideas.one_liner: A quarterly shadow NAV and gate-probability score for every non-traded BDC and interval fund, sold to the RIAs and OCIOs who put clients into them.
ideas.customer: Independent RIAs and family offices ($100M to $3B AUM) with client money in non-traded BDCs, interval and tender-offer funds, at $400 to $1,500 per month per firm. Secondary buyers are TAMPs and wealth platforms (API license) and 401(k) advisers as alternatives enter defined-contribution plans.
ideas.problem: Advisers learn a fund has gated from a sponsor letter after the tender window closes. In Q1 2026 non-traded BDC investors requested about $13.9B and got about $7.4B. Blackstone gated BCRED in June 2026 with about 5% fills, and Q2 requests hit a record 12.4% of NAV with only 38% filled. Reported NAVs are smoothed, and nobody tells an adviser whether the next tender will be pro-rated or what to file.
ideas.solution: Ingest the tender-offer filings (window and cap), 10-Q and N-PORT marks, non-accruals and PIK share, listed-BDC discount to NAV, secondary bids on non-traded shares, and loan-index prices. Output three things per fund: (1) shadow NAV against reported NAV, (2) probability that the next tender gates and the expected fill rate, (3) a 'if I request X, expect to receive Y' calculator. Add compliance-ready client letters. Start as a public tracker of about 40 funds, then put the alerts and calculator behind a paywall.
ideas.why_now: 2026 is the first year pro-rata gating hit the whole non-traded BDC category. Blue Owl merged a non-traded BDC into its listed sibling under redemption pressure. The August 2025 executive order opening 401(k)s to alternatives is about to push far more retail money into these wrappers. Private-credit blowups in late 2025 turned advisers from curious to scared.
ideas.revenue_model: Tiered subscription for advisers, an enterprise API for wealth platforms and TAMPs, and a $250 per-fund 'client-ready due diligence memo' for compliance files.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Pro-rata gating makes over-requesting the dominant strategy. Once investors expect a 14 to 38 cent fill, they file bigger requests than they need, so request size becomes a self-amplifying signal. It overstates true demand but predicts fill rates well. The gap between the listed-BDC discount and reported NAV leads request size by about a quarter. Quants see this as a bank-run game with strategic complements, not a credit-loss story, and nobody in wealth tech models it that way.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape EDGAR tender-offer, 10-Q and N-PORT filings for about 40 funds and publish a free weekly 'gate watch' on LinkedIn and Substack framed as research. DM 100 RIA compliance heads and CIOs. Convert 10 to a $500-per-month pilot and start talks with two wealth-platform data teams.

ideas.title: Tariff Refund Claim Files for Small Importers
ideas.one_liner: Turn a small importer's messy customs data into a refund-ready, financeable claim ledger, paid by success fee or on sale of the claim.
ideas.customer: US importers of record with roughly $50K to $5M of IEEPA duties who lack in-house customs staff, plus the licensed customs brokers serving them. Claim-buying funds and lenders are the second payer, paying a per-file diligence fee.
ideas.problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026 and the CIT ordered refunds. CBP's CAPE tool has accepted about $134.7B of the roughly $166B pool as of September 11, 2026. The tail sits with the smallest importers. Their ACE accounts are unapproved, they missed the 90-day request window, or their entries are liquidated beyond the 80-day reprocessing window, which the DOJ is appealing at the Federal Circuit. Phase 3, for liquidated entries, was slated for October 6 but delayed. Many are selling claims at deep discounts out of fear or confusion.
ideas.solution: Ingest ACE entry-summary reports, broker CSVs and payment records. Map every line to the IEEPA HTS 9903 lines. Compute per-entry phase eligibility, liquidation dates and protest deadlines. Flag duplicate or wrong importer-of-record entries, drawback and FTZ overlaps, and interest owed. Output CAPE-ready batches plus a chain-of-title 'claim data room' with a probability-weighted value for the appeal-dependent entries. A licensed broker partner files, so the product stays software plus workflow. The same engine reprocesses future tariff refunds and exclusions.
ideas.why_now: The window is open now: CAPE phases run through fall 2026, the Federal Circuit appeal will set the value of the liquidated tail, and hedge funds and lenders are already buying refund claims. Successor tariffs under other statutes create the same entry-level data problem next year.
ideas.revenue_model: 8 to 12% success fee on refunds recovered. A 2 to 4% origination fee when a claim is sold or financed. $500 to $2,000 per-claim diligence files sold to buyers. A subscription for customs brokers who use it across their book.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Distressed-claims desks (Lehman, FTX, Celsius trade claims) know a claim's price is set less by the underlying merits than by documentation quality, chain of title and timing. Whoever standardizes the data room becomes the market's gatekeeper. The small-importer tail is mispriced because sellers can't prove what they are owed, and buyers can't underwrite what they can't verify. The moat is the underwriting file, not the filing.
ideas.first_30_days: Build an ES-003 and ACE CSV parser with two or three friendly licensed customs brokers. Offer a free 'refund gap audit' to 30 small importers found through public importer lists. Sign 10 on contingency. Get letters of intent from one or two claim buyers wanting standardized diligence files.

ideas.title: Resolution-Risk Ratings for Prediction Market Contracts
ideas.one_liner: A credit-rating-style score for how likely an event contract is to resolve ambiguously or be disputed, plus the rulebook basis between 'identical' contracts on different venues.
ideas.customer: Prop desks, market makers and arbitrage funds trading Kalshi, Polymarket and newer venues, at $300 to $3,000 per month. Venues and market creators pay for pre-listing rule linting.
ideas.problem: Polymarket logged more than 1,150 disputed markets in the first half of 2026, more than all of 2025. A US-Iran peace-deal market with over $345M in volume split traders on whether the outcome met a 'permanent' deal. Cross-venue arbitrage is not risk-free because sources, cutoffs and definitions differ, and displayed depth can vanish. Everyone prices the event, but nobody prices the contract wording.
ideas.solution: Parse each contract's rules (source of truth, timestamp cutoff, key definitions) and compare against a labeled history of disputes and oracle overrides. Output a 0-100 Resolution Risk Score with an expected haircut in cents. Give matched cross-venue pairs a scenario table of where they would settle differently, so arbitrageurs size positions correctly. Offer a 'rule linter' that flags ambiguous phrases for market creators, and deliver everything through an API and Discord/Telegram alerts.
ideas.why_now: Prediction-market volume is exploding (Kalshi reportedly passed $100B) and dispute counts are rising sharply. Institutional market makers are arriving and need risk inputs beyond price. Regulators and states are still fighting over these contracts, so rulebook and venue risk is priced by no one.
ideas.revenue_model: Desk subscriptions, per-market audit or lint fees from venues and market creators, and a data license to aggregators and terminals.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Credit derivatives already lived through this. The asset's definition, meaning restructuring clauses and Determinations Committee rulings, became a priced factor, and an entire professional infrastructure grew around it. Prediction markets are at the 2003 CDS stage: the basis between 'identical' instruments is definitional risk. The winner is the rating-agency-plus-dispute-committee layer, not another odds aggregator.
ideas.first_30_days: Scrape resolved and disputed markets and hand-label about 300 disputes into an ambiguity taxonomy. Publish a public weekly 'Dispute Watch' with two or three calls that prove right. Sell to five arbitrage-bot shops through their Discord and Telegram communities at $500 per month. Offer free linting to prolific market creators for testimonials.

ideas.title: Point-in-Time Certification for Alternative Data Vendors
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-paid, buyer-trusted forensic test that a dataset's history is genuinely point-in-time, extended to certify that an LLM-driven signal isn't leaking hindsight, plus a cheap timestamp 'witness' service.
ideas.customer: Mid-sized alt-data vendors and AI-signal startups ($2M to $50M ARR) selling to funds, at $15K to $40K per certification, about $8K per year to recertify, and $500 per month for the witness service. Fund data-sourcing teams use the reports free, which is what makes the badge valuable.
ideas.problem: Quants ask every vendor one question: 'when did you start collecting live?' The honest answer is usually that the history was reconstructed, with today's entity maps and taxonomies, overwritten revisions, and publication timestamps standing in for availability timestamps. Funds burn three to six months of trials before discovering this. Vendors lose deals, and every fund duplicates the same diligence. LLM signals add parametric hindsight, where the model's weights already know the outcomes of the backtest period.
ideas.solution: A standardized battery run on vendor samples under NDA. It tests for discontinuities at the claimed live date (coverage, missingness, revision rates, distribution shifts, entity-map consistency, timestamp-lag distribution) and for survivorship and delisting gaps. For LLM signals it runs black-box hindsight probes and entity-masked or post-cutoff re-runs. The output is a PIT Grade, a one-page badge and a machine-readable report. The witness service takes a daily cryptographic hash or snapshot of the vendor's feed, so in a year the vendor has third-party-provable live history.
ideas.why_now: Thousands of data vendors now sell into funds, banks and AI-agent builders who lack quant-grade diligence. 2025 to 2026 research (Look-Ahead-Bench, HindsightBench, detecting lookahead in LLM forecasts) has made LLM look-ahead bias a mainstream worry. Regulators are scrutinizing hypothetical and backtested performance claims.
ideas.revenue_model: Issuer-pays certification fees, annual recertification, a per-month witness subscription, and a premium hindsight audit for AI-signal vendors and allocators diligencing AI-driven funds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The only real proof of point-in-time history is a third party's timestamps, because vendor engineers routinely overwrite and backfill. Each buyer rediscovers this privately, so the cost is duplicated across hundreds of funds. Shifting the cost to the vendor, who wants the shorter sales cycle, is the arbitrage. Credibility requires published methodology and public aggregate fail rates, or it becomes a pay-for-grade scheme like pre-2008 ratings.
ideas.first_30_days: Open-source the PIT test suite on GitHub and publish teardowns of three public datasets. Get two or three fund data-sourcing heads to say they would use the reports. Sell five vendors a $7.5K 'pre-audit' in exchange for being named references, and launch the witness hash service to any vendor who asks.

ideas.title: Peak-Load Call Service for Mid-Size Factories
ideas.one_liner: Predict the handful of hours a year that set a facility's capacity charge and alert the plant manager to cut load, paid as a share of verified savings.
ideas.customer: Commercial and industrial sites of 300 kW to 5 MW in PJM (and ERCOT 4CP) territories that demand-response aggregators ignore: cold storage, water and wastewater plants, plastics and aggregates producers, ice rinks and indoor farms. Energy brokers and consultants are the channel.
ideas.problem: A customer's capacity tag (PLC) is set by usage during a few system-peak hours, and its cost then sits on every bill for a year. PJM capacity prices have risen roughly tenfold since 2024/25, with recent auctions clearing at the cap of about $330/MW-day, so a 1 MW site's tag is worth six figures. Owners either never curtail and overpay, or curtail on 20+ hot days and lose production. Aggregators skim 20 to 40% and focus on large accounts.
ideas.solution: Model the probability that each upcoming hour ranks in the system's top peaks for the site's zone or utility rules. Use weather ensembles, load forecasts, calendar effects and, critically, the season's running maximum so far. Send a text or BMS signal with the expected value of curtailing against the plant's own curtailment cost. Cut curtailment days from about 25 to about 8 and stop alerting once the peaks have been 'caught'.
ideas.why_now: Data-center load growth has pushed PJM capacity clearing prices to the cap two auctions in a row, and those costs are now hitting commercial bills. Open AI weather ensembles (ECMWF AIFS, NOAA) make sharper probabilistic forecasts cheap. The just-finished 2026 summer is fresh evidence for a backtest pitch.
ideas.revenue_model: 20 to 25% of verified savings (measured from the next year's PLC change), a $250 to $500 monthly alert subscription, and $2K to $5K paid load audits. Brokers and consultants get a channel rebate.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Quants see 'top 5 hours out of 4,000' as an order-statistics and optimal-stopping problem with asymmetric payoffs, not a pure forecasting problem. As the season's record load rises, the threshold to enter the top 5 becomes known, the option value of alerts collapses, and you can stop curtailing early. Incumbents earn more the more events they call, so their models over-alert. The savings show up a year later on an invoice nobody links to behavior, so customers underinvest without a counterfactual 'what your tag would have been' report.
ideas.first_30_days: Use the off-season to pull public PJM hourly load and zonal data, backtest 2019 to 2026 peaks, and generate a free 'what your tag would have been' report for 100 facilities found through EIA and utility-tariff lists. Sell $3K load audits to the first five, sign shared-savings pilots for summer 2027, and recruit two energy brokers as channel partners.

ideas.title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
ideas.customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
ideas.problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
ideas.solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
ideas.why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.

ideas.title: The Recorder's Rulebook: Avalara for the Recording Counter
ideas.one_liner: A verified, machine-readable rulebook and fee oracle for every recording jurisdiction, with a preflight checker that tells you a document will be rejected before you send it.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size title and escrow agencies, estate-planning and real estate attorneys, HOA and property managers, lenders' closing teams, and later closing-software and e-recording platforms that embed the API. Counties get listed free.
ideas.problem: There are roughly 3,600 recording jurisdictions, each with its own margins, font sizes, notary wording, parcel-ID format, cover sheets, per-page fees, surcharges and transfer taxes. Those rules sit on stale county web pages and in clerks' heads. Rejections delay closings two to seven days, burn recorder staff time on every bounce, and wrong fee estimates create TRID tolerance problems for lenders. Fees also keep moving as counties backfill shrinking recording revenue (Wayne County MI has floated a $30 fee increase, Montana raised per-page fees, and other counties report seven-figure losses tied to fee changes).
ideas.solution: A crowd-verified rulebook per county and document type. A PDF preflight scans geometry (margins, fonts, blank space), notary block completeness, legal description, APN format and preparer and return-to fields, and returns specific fixes. A to-the-penny fee and transfer-tax calculator handles every surcharge. A change log tracks statute changes and effective dates (many take effect July 1 or January 1). Each county gets a one-click quarterly 'attest my page' link, which clerks will use because every rejection costs them 15-30 minutes plus postage. Start as a free 'will this be rejected?' web checker to collect users, then sell API access.
ideas.why_now: Recording volumes have been depressed since 2022 and counties are raising fees, which makes fee tables stale. Remote online notarization and e-recording put far more documents in front of closers who have never met the county's quirks. Title staff attrition means fewer people who just know the rules. Vision-capable LLMs make geometry and notary-block checks cheap for the first time.
ideas.revenue_model: $1-$3 per preflight check plus $99-$499/month tiers for agencies. Per-call API pricing for closing platforms and e-recording vendors, and a data license for lenders needing accurate recording-fee and transfer-tax estimates.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Clerks reject because the stamp is a legal act, not because we are picky. The top ten rejection reasons are identical everywhere, but the thresholds differ, and most bounces come from occasional submitters (attorneys, HOA managers, individuals), not the big title companies that already have local runners. The moat is not software, it is the boring verified dataset, and clerks will help you build it because they are the ones who suffer from the bounces.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with an active recorders' association and build the full rulebook for 25 counties by phone and web, with a clerk sign-off on each. Ship the free checker, promote it through the association newsletter and estate-planning attorney groups, and convert the heaviest users to a $99/month plan. Approach a closing-software partner program once you have about 200 active users.

ideas.title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
ideas.one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
ideas.customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
ideas.problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
ideas.solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
ideas.why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
ideas.revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.

ideas.title: Boundary Truth: Ledger of Special-District Lines
ideas.one_liner: Turn recorded annexation, inclusion and exclusion instruments into a single authoritative boundary ledger that catches wrong tax bills, wrong ballots and wrong 911 routing.
ideas.customer: County assessors and treasurers, election offices, state 911 boards and NG911 GIS coordinators, plus special-district management firms and metro-district law firms. Paid through the recorder's technology or preservation fund (spendable at the recorder's discretion in many states), election grant money or 911 fee funds.
ideas.problem: There are about 39,000 special districts (fire, water, library, mosquito, metro) and their boundary changes are recorded with the county clerk as ministerial filings with no downstream notification. Nobody reliably updates the assessor's tax-area codes, the election office's address-to-district crosswalk or the 911 emergency-service boundary layer. Result: parcels billed by the wrong district or by none (lost revenue, later refunds), voters handed the wrong ballot style, and dispatch mismatches. State attorneys general have issued opinions on tax levies made after officials weren't notified of boundary changes. We discover the errors in the last two weeks before an election or when a taxpayer complains.
ideas.solution: An AI pipeline reads the recorded instruments (metes-and-bounds text, plats, ordinances), draws polygons with closure and area sanity checks, and routes low-confidence ones to a human reviewer. It keeps a versioned, effective-dated ledger of each district's legal boundary. It then diffs the ledger against the assessor's tax-area file, the voter address crosswalk and the 911 boundary layer, and returns a plain exception list such as '312 parcels inside Fire District 4 per the 2022 recorded inclusion but billed to no district.' Sell a fixed-price audit first, then an annual subscription.
ideas.why_now: Mid-decade redistricting fights and the 2026 midterms have made ballot-style accuracy politically radioactive. NG911 requires clean authoritative boundary GIS data. Property tax scrutiny makes every misbilled dollar a headline. LLMs can now parse legal descriptions well enough to draft polygons that a human reviews rather than draws.
ideas.revenue_model: $15k-$40k one-time boundary drift audit per county, then $10k-$30k/year per county for continuous monitoring, sized to fit inside a recorder's technology fund or a 911 board budget. Data-quality add-ons for district management firms and bond counsel.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The legal boundary is the recorded instrument, not the GIS layer; the layer is just someone's drawing of a PDF. Because the clerk often sits at the junction of records, elections and sometimes tax, we see the stale cascade that assessors, election staff and 911 GIS analysts each see only a slice of. Also, the clerk's tech fund often sits outside the commissioners' budget fight, so a $25k audit can be approved in weeks, not the 18 months that scares govtech investors.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state heavy on special districts (Colorado metro districts, Texas MUDs and ESDs, Illinois, Washington, Florida CDDs). Offer a free boundary drift audit to a single county's assessor and clerk using five years of recorded inclusions and annexations. Turn the mismatch list into a paid pilot funded from the recorder's fund, then take the proof to the state 911 board.

ideas.title: One-Filing Shield for At-Risk Public Servants
ideas.one_liner: A single intake that files every county office's address-confidentiality forms, fixes what gets recorded next, and monitors leaks for judges, election officials and clinicians.
ideas.customer: County and municipal risk pools and insurers, state associations of election officials, clerks, judges and school boards, hospital systems and physician groups (employer benefit), and police unions. Paid per protected person per year.
ideas.problem: A determined stalker can find almost anyone's home address in 30 seconds through deeds, the assessor roll, the voter file, court files, marriage licenses and business filings. Confidentiality and redaction laws now exist in 30+ states, but each office (recorder, assessor, treasurer, court clerk, voter registration, business filings) has its own form and process, and none talk to each other. Redaction usually masks the online index while the image stays retrievable at the counter and in bulk data purchases, so people-search brokers re-scrape it. Broker-removal services only hit the last layer. Clerks are ministerial and legally barred from advising anyone, so nobody explains the fix.
ideas.solution: A concierge plus software product. One intake produces and files every state- and county-specific confidentiality request across all relevant offices, with notary and wet-ink logistics handled. A local attorney network handles retitling into a privacy land trust or LLC with agent-signed deeds and mailing-address-only recording before anything new is recorded. It moves the voter registration to protected status, scrubs business filings, monitors new recordings and assessor changes monthly for the client's name, and runs broker takedowns as a final layer. Publish a free county-by-county confidentiality forms map as the top-of-funnel.
ideas.why_now: The June 2025 Minnesota lawmaker shootings, in which the suspect allegedly used people-search sites to compile officials' addresses, pushed a wave of new laws. California AB 302 requires deletions within five days from August 1, 2026, and Delaware, Florida and Georgia have judge-protection statutes. Threats against election officials and the November 3, 2026 midterms keep the issue hot, and insurers are pushing risk mitigation onto pools and employers.
ideas.revenue_model: $180-$450 per protected person per year as a benefit purchased by pools, associations or employers, plus a one-time onboarding fee and attorney-fulfilled trust-deed packages at cost plus margin. Group pricing for a pool covering hundreds of officials.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Redaction in a county system is a display mask, not deletion, so the leak returns through the image and bulk data. The real protection is changing what gets recorded before it is recorded, which is precisely what a clerk cannot tell anyone. The 'first mile' data source is the county, not the broker, and nobody in the privacy-service industry works the six separate county offices.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state with a friendly clerks' association and do concierge onboarding at cost for about 20 county clerks and election officials through that association. Publish the county-by-county forms map to earn trust and backlinks. Pitch one county risk pool a 100-person pilot at $250 per person, line up one local attorney for the trust-deed workflow, and collect testimonials from the first cohort.

ideas.title: Ex-Botter Red Team for Limited Drops
ideas.one_liner: Pay former sneaker-bot users to attack your product drop before launch, then rent you the checkout filter that stops what they found.
ideas.customer: Indie brands that run limited drops on Shopify with 500 to 5,000 units: streetwear labels, collectible toy and art-toy makers, TCG shops, sneaker boutiques, merch stores, small beauty and food brands. They pay $750 to $2,500 per pentest, then a per-drop or monthly fee.
ideas.problem: Brands think a waiting room or Cloudflare stops scalpers. It only stops speed. Real resellers win by multiplying identities, not by being fast. They use Gmail dot and plus tricks and catch-all domains, address jigging (Apt vs Unit vs #, an extra letter in the street name), virtual cards from one issuer, and residential proxies. One 'customer' becomes 40 orders. Fans get nothing, the brand gets angry DMs, and the resale premium goes to strangers. Small brands cannot afford enterprise bot vendors and do not know what to look for.
ideas.solution: Wedge: a 'Drop Pentest'. We run a real reseller stack against the brand's store or staging a week before launch and hand back a report: 'we would have captured 38% of your units, here is how'. Product: a Shopify checkout app called One Per Human. It normalizes emails, fuzzy-dedupes addresses (USPS-style standardization plus apartment and unit variants), clusters card fingerprints and BINs, phone-verifies and blocks VoIP numbers, and flags or auto-cancels suspected multiples before fulfillment, with a human review queue. Optional 'verified reseller tier' at a higher price so the brand captures some of the flip premium legitimately.
ideas.why_now: Collectible drops have become a public mess in 2025-26: Labubu and other Pop Mart drops, and Pokemon TCG releases where stores had fights, lines, and pulled product. Indie brands now copy sneaker-style drops, with sneaker-style bot pressure. Cheap LLM fuzzy matching makes address and identity dedupe far cheaper to build than it was two years ago. Shopify's checkout extensibility gives apps a place to validate or flag orders.
ideas.revenue_model: Pentest at $750 to $2,500. Guard app at $149 to $499 per drop, or 0.5% to 1% of drop GMV. Annual contracts for brands that drop monthly.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Bots do not beat drops on speed. They beat them on identity multiplication, and the tells sit in the order data (address shape, email pattern, card issuer clusters) that the brand already has. Only someone who has run the tricks knows which tells matter. The poacher-turned-gamekeeper credibility is the moat, and the pentest report sells the product by showing the brand its own leak.
ideas.first_30_days: Days 1 to 7: build the attack checklist from what I and my Discord friends already do. Days 7 to 14: DM 100 small Shopify brands with an upcoming drop on Instagram, offering a free mini-audit built from their public store, such as how easy it is to create fake variants of an address. Days 14 to 30: convert 3 to 5 into paid pentests at $750 and use the findings to pre-sell the app. Delivery is mostly a spreadsheet plus screenshots.

ideas.title: Restock Monitors Turned Competitor Sell-Through Radar
ideas.one_liner: Repurpose the Discord restock-monitor infrastructure teen resellers run into a SKU- and size-level sell-through index for DTC brands and the investors and acquirers who buy them.
ideas.customer: Founders and merchandisers of DTC brands who want to see rivals' sell-through ($199 to $799 per month), boutique retail buyers, and consumer-focused funds, search-fund buyers and e-commerce acquirers who need diligence on a Shopify brand ($2,000 to $5,000 per report).
ideas.problem: Everyone in e-commerce has to guess how fast a competitor's hero product actually sells. Public analytics tools give traffic estimates, not sell-through by size, color or restock. Buyers of small Shopify brands take the seller's word for 'we sell out in days' and get burned.
ideas.solution: Teen resellers already run monitors on thousands of storefronts: each one polls public product feeds so a Discord ping fires the instant a size restocks. The same stream, kept as history, shows how fast each variant flips to sold-out, restock cadence, drop timing, markdown timing, price changes and collection moves. Package it as a weekly Sold-Out Index and an on-demand brand report: 'their black M hoodie sold out in 41 minutes twice, restocked every 3 weeks, and they cut price 15% after the tariff news'. Use public storefront signals only, with no checkout tricks, and honor rate limits and terms.
ideas.why_now: Tariff-driven price changes in 2025-26 have every brand asking what rivals did to prices and when. DTC brand acquisition and roll-up activity means more diligence is being done on tiny Shopify brands. LLMs now classify messy product titles into a clean taxonomy cheaply, which was the hard part of turning monitor pings into an index.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscription for brand and retail buyers ($199 to $799 per month), one-off diligence reports ($2,000 to $5,000), and a data feed for funds later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The restock-alert economy is really an accidental, huge, always-on sensor network for the long tail of DTC commerce. Enterprise alt-data vendors ignore small brands because they think there is no data on them. Resellers have been logging exactly that data every minute for years. The unit of value is sold-out speed by variant, which reseller monitors track and analytics vendors do not.
ideas.first_30_days: Take the existing monitor feed for about 2,000 storefronts in streetwear, sneakers and collectibles and start logging history now, because history is the asset. Publish a free weekly Sold-Out Index thread on TikTok and X to get inbound. Sell 10 founders a $199 competitor watchlist by DM. Pitch one search-fund or acquirer community for a paid diligence report at $2,000 to check willingness to pay.

ideas.title: Hype-Item Triage for Thrift and Charity Shops
ideas.one_liner: A 10-second back-room scan station that tells thrift and charity staff which donated sneakers and collectibles are worth $150 instead of $12, then lists them online for a revenue share.
ideas.customer: Independent Goodwill regionals, church and charity thrift shops, Plato's Closet-style franchisees, consignment shops and estate-sale companies. They pay a rev share on the uplift, or $199 per month per store.
ideas.problem: Thrift pricers are paid to move volume and price shoes at a flat $8 to $25 by category. Meanwhile teen and adult resellers ('pickers') walk the racks right after restock and buy the $12 pairs worth $200 and up. Donations are the shop's raw material, and the shop is giving the profit to the pickers. Charities lose real money, and staff cannot read a style code or tell a real pair from a fake, so they either underprice or avoid the risk.
ideas.solution: A tablet at the sorting table. Staff photograph the tongue tag or box label. OCR pulls the style code and size, then the app returns resale value, days-to-sell, condition-adjusted price and known fake tells for that model. Anything over $60 goes into an 'online' bin. Our remote team of college and teen resellers lists, ships and remits the shop's share, so the shop needs no e-commerce staff. Later categories: trading cards, LEGO, vintage tees, Stanley cups, Pokemon sealed product, watches.
ideas.why_now: Thrift has boomed with Gen Z while tariffs push shoppers to secondhand, which also means more pickers hitting the same racks. Multimodal models now read tag photos accurately and cheaply. Donations arrive in volume, but shop margins are squeezed by picker competition and labor costs. Charities have never had a hype-specific tool.
ideas.revenue_model: 20% to 30% of net sale price on items routed to online, or a SaaS fee per store. Charities are motivated because it is found money for their programs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The biggest sneaker sourcing channel for resellers is a flat-price system that cannot see value. The knowledge needed is tiny: style code, size, box, one authenticity tell. That is why resellers win, and it can be sold to the seller side. Being reseller-native gives me trust with staff and the sourcing instincts to know which categories are next.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer three local charity thrift shops a free two-week pilot. I sort through their back room on a Saturday, list the top 30 items, and split proceeds with the charity (charity 70%, us 30%). Track the uplift versus what those items would have sold for on the floor. Turn the numbers into a one-page case study and pitch 20 more independent thrift operators.

ideas.title: Pallet Co-Op for Micro-Resellers
ideas.one_liner: A distributor for one-person resellers that buys store-closing truckloads, values them SKU by SKU, and splits them into size-matched $150 to $500 shares delivered to each member.
ideas.customer: Under-25 and hobbyist resellers (roughly 3 to 100 sales per week) who currently buy at retail or from other resellers. They pay a markup of 8% to 15% plus a $19 per month membership.
ideas.problem: Real wholesale margins are locked behind minimum order quantities and size-run mismatch. A liquidator lot has 240 pairs, but 60% are size 6 or size 13 that nobody wants to hold. Mystery pallets are priced as a percentage of MSRP, not by what a SKU actually resells for, so buyers overpay for junk and underbid the winners. Discord 'group buys' exist but run on trust and screenshots, and they collapse when someone ghosts on payment.
ideas.solution: We buy truckload and pallet lots from liquidators and closing retailers, run the manifest against resale comps to price every line, and slice it: each member gets a share of the SKUs and sizes they selected, with the top-value pairs allocated by lottery so nobody feels cheated. Deposits are collected before we buy, so we carry almost no inventory risk. A partnered 3PL or a garage-and-labels crew ships each member's slice within a week. Later: net-14 financing on shares and buy-back of unsold slow-moving sizes.
ideas.why_now: Retail contraction is producing a steady stream of liquidation lots in 2025-26: Foot Locker is being folded into Dick's with store consolidation, other mall and footwear chains are closing doors, and brands reset inventory after tariff and demand swings. Margins on hyped Nike pairs are thin, so only good buying keeps micro-resellers alive. Cheap vision models make manifest-to-comp valuation nearly free.
ideas.revenue_model: 8% to 15% markup on each share plus $19 per month membership. Later, interest on short-term inventory financing and fees for a 'sell-through insurance' tier.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Capital is not what stops small resellers from wholesale. Break-bulk is. Nobody sells a truckload in 40 slices sorted by size. The person who does the boring sorting, allocating and shipping becomes the small reseller's Costco. Because valuation uses resale comps rather than MSRP percent, the co-op can quietly outbid mystery-pallet buyers on the best lots.
ideas.first_30_days: Find one liquidator willing to sell a 5 to 10 pallet lot of mixed sneakers and apparel. Pre-sell 40 slots at $250 each in a Discord with deposits before buying anything, using the manifest value as the pitch. Rent a garage or use a local prep center. Ship in 10 days, collect testimonials and reviews, then run the next lot every week.

ideas.title: Founder File for Under-18 Hustlers
ideas.one_liner: A verified business transcript, tax pack and Roth IRA earned-income record for the parents of teens who legally can't hold the seller accounts their income runs through.
ideas.customer: Parents of 14 to 17-year-old sellers (eBay, StockX, GOAT, Whatnot, TikTok Shop, Depop, Shopify), high-school entrepreneurship programs (DECA, FBLA, Junior Achievement, NFTE), and college counselors. $12 to $15 per month or $149 per year, or $5 per student through programs.
ideas.problem: Most major marketplaces require sellers to be 18, so teens run their business under a parent's ID and account. The income, cost basis and reputation all legally belong to the parent. The parent gets a 1099-K on gross sales with no cost basis, which looks like profit. The kid can't prove any of it on a college application, and nobody is documenting the earned income that would let the family fund a custodial Roth IRA (contribution capped at the lower of earned income or the annual limit, roughly $7,000 to $7,500 per year).
ideas.solution: Founder File connects read-only to platform exports, PayPal and Gmail receipts, matches purchases to sales for cost basis, and produces: (1) a signed Business Transcript PDF for Common App activity entries and scholarship applications, (2) a Schedule C-ready summary and quarterly estimates for the parent, reviewed by a partner CPA, (3) an earned-income letter and referral to Fidelity or Schwab custodial Roth accounts, and (4) an '18th birthday migration' kit to move history to the kid's own accounts.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 tax law rolled the 1099-K reporting threshold back toward $20,000 and 200 transactions, so many teen sellers land in a confusing gray zone about reporting. College admissions increasingly reward proof of real work as test-optional policies spread and AI-polished essays get discounted. Teen commerce through TikTok Shop, Whatnot and reselling is at its peak, and Gen Alpha hustle culture is pulling younger kids in.
ideas.revenue_model: Parent subscription, per-student pricing through school programs, and referral fees from custodial brokerage accounts. Possible upsell: CPA-reviewed tax filing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Teen resellers are among the most under-documented earned-income earners in the country. Documenting what they already do unlocks tax-free compounding worth thousands per kid and turns a bedroom hobby into an admissions asset. The buyer is the parent, who pays for college advantage without hesitation, while everyone else sells to the kid.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 teen resellers from the Discord servers I am in. Give them free transcripts in return for parent-approved testimonials. Have a CPA friend sign off on a template. Sell a $49 'Transcript plus Roth IRA setup' bundle to their parents, and offer the transcript to 5 college-counseling and 'teen entrepreneur' TikTok creators for an affiliate cut.

ideas.title: Recorded Parent Voices, Endowed to Outlive Us
ideas.one_liner: Guided, human-only voice and video milestone messages for the children of dying parents, with the hosting prepaid so the recordings outlive the company.
ideas.customer: Terminally ill parents of minor children, or their spouses. Referrals come from oncology and young-adult cancer social workers, child-life specialists, and hospice social workers. Hospice foundations sponsor families who cannot pay.
ideas.problem: Dying parents of young children want to leave their actual voice for the 16th birthday, the wedding and the first heartbreak. They start too late. By the time hospice admission happens, many patients are too sedated, breathless or confused to record anything usable. The generic tools (StoryWorth-style prompts, phone voice memos) produce rambling, prompt-less files. Families also do not trust vendors to still exist in 20 years. Meanwhile AI voice-cloning 'deadbots' are being pitched at the same families, and most of them recoil.
ideas.solution: A two-session guided capture (in person or on video) run by a trained 'legacy guide' with a chaplain or child-bereavement background. It uses a prompt library organized by the child's future age: what a 12-year-old needs to hear versus a 30-year-old. Examples: 'how I met your dad', 'what I was afraid of', 'what I'd say when you're furious at me', and a mundane category (how I laughed, my opinion of your first crush) that grown children say matters most. The output is edited, human-only audio and video with a strict no-synthesis policy. Each message is tagged to a milestone and delivered by the surviving guardian's app. There is a physical archival copy and printed transcripts. Hosting is prepaid into a trust-held reserve, with a contractual right to export everything if the company dies. Durability and authenticity are the product, not features.
ideas.why_now: AI voice-cloning is now cheap and good enough that grief-tech is being flooded with synthetic 'talk to your dead mom' products. Public and clinical unease about them is rising, which opens a clear 'only what they actually said' position. At least some early digital-afterlife vendors have folded or pivoted, so buyers are primed to ask 'will this exist in 2045?'. Phone-quality recording is now good enough that no studio is needed. I could not verify specific vendor failures in this session, so confirm before using them in marketing.
ideas.revenue_model: Roughly $450 for guided capture plus a one-time $600 to $900 permanence endowment (about $1,000 to $1,400 per family). The endowment funds 30-year hosting, and the reserve is held in a trust or escrow. Add-ons: printed keepsake book, extra milestone messages, and an 'audio blessing' set for each child. Hospice and hospital foundations sponsor uninsured families at a discounted wholesale rate.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The market timing is wrong in everyone's mind. The recording window closes weeks before hospice, so the referral source is oncology, not hospice. What dying parents fear most is not death but vanishing, and that includes the file vanishing. Buyers will pay more for a credible 'this outlives our company' promise than for any feature. Refusing to synthesize is a selling point that families and chaplains will repeat.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit two oncology or child-life social workers as design partners. Run 8 to 10 free pilot sessions using a phone and a $60 lavalier mic, and write the age-banded prompt library from what the kids' guardians say they'd want. Get a small-estates attorney or trust company to set up the escrow and export-if-we-fail clause. Put up a one-page site, then charge from case 11. Ask the first families for a written testimonial and referrals to two other oncology units.

ideas.title: After-Death Home Reset for Hospice Families
ideas.one_liner: A two-person crew that returns the house to normal within 48 hours of a home hospice death: bed out, meds destroyed, room restored, memory box packed.
ideas.customer: Hospice agencies pay per home death, as a family-experience and bereavement differentiator. A second stream is families paying a premium, and funeral homes reselling it as an add-on.
ideas.problem: After a home death the hospital bed, oxygen concentrator and commode often sit in the living room for days. The DME vendor schedules pickup on its own clock. The leftover morphine, lorazepam and haloperidol 'comfort kit' sits in the fridge or cabinet. Nurses are supposed to see to disposal, but the home visit is often skipped or rushed, and families quietly keep or mis-dispose of them. The dead person's glasses, dentures and hearing aids end up in a drawer. The family remembers the empty bed in the middle of the room for the rest of their lives. The CAHPS Hospice family survey arrives months later and those last impressions color the answers.
ideas.solution: A chaplain-designed protocol delivered by two trained, background-checked staff in a branded van. On admission, the hospice photographs the room so the crew can restore the original furniture layout. Within 24 to 48 hours of death the crew coordinates or performs bed and equipment removal, destroys leftover controlled drugs with deactivation pouches and a witnessed log the hospice can put in the chart, and launders linens. They pack a memory box (glasses, jewelry, a worn shirt, the last handwritten note). They restore the room, open the windows, and offer a two-minute optional blessing or silence. A hand-off card tells the family what happens at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
ideas.why_now: Hospice is consolidating, with private equity and large chains competing on public CAHPS-based quality scores that drive referrals. Regulators and communities are paying more attention to opioid diversion. Hospice per-diem margins are squeezed and the DME vendors they use are getting slower and cheaper. Home is where most hospice deaths occur. Also, nurses are stretched thin, so the care they used to give informally in that first day is disappearing, and nobody owns it.
ideas.revenue_model: Hospice pays $250 to $400 per home death on a per-case contract, with volume tiers. Families or funeral homes pay $450 to $600 for a premium version with a full room refresh and donation pickup for clothing and mobility aids. A hospice with roughly 100 patients on service has on the order of 25 to 35 deaths a month, around half at home, so three hospices support a small crew. Sponsorship from a nonprofit hospice foundation can cover indigent families.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the crisis is the moment of death. Insiders know the emotional injury persists in the physical room and in the loose ends nobody owns: the bed, the drugs, the dentures. The hospice would love to solve it but cannot bill for it and the nurse has already left. Whoever owns hours 6 through 48 after death, when the funeral home has taken the body and all clinical staff have gone, owns the family's memory of the hospice.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one small nonprofit hospice as a design partner. Write the checklist with the chaplain, the DON and a pharmacist for the controlled-drug disposal log. Buy a used van, get general liability coverage, and hire two people with home-health-aide or hospitality backgrounds. Do the first 5 to 8 resets free in exchange for family feedback. Charge from case 9, and ask the hospice's quality director to compare family feedback scores with and without the reset.

ideas.title: Widowhood Risk Program Sold to Medicare Payers
ideas.one_liner: Use hospice's early knowledge that a caregiver spouse is about to become a widow to enroll them in a 180-day protective program, paid for by Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs.
ideas.customer: Medicare Advantage plans (especially those with dual-eligible special needs plans), ACOs and value-based primary care groups. Hospice agencies are the intake channel and receive a referral or administrative fee.
ideas.problem: The spouse of a hospice patient is the second patient, and nobody is paid to treat them. The caregiver spouse ran the pillbox, the checkbook, the driving and the meals. They have skipped their own appointments for months. In the weeks after the funeral their chronic conditions decompensate, and hospitalizations, ED visits and falls spike. The chaplain is the one person who sees the untouched pills, the empty refrigerator and the missed doctor visits. Payers only learn of the death through enrollment data that lags by weeks or months. Hospice bereavement services are a mailing program, and they do not bill for the spouse's medical risk.
ideas.solution: A two-part program. Before the death, a hospice chaplain or social worker flags a high-risk caregiver spouse using a 6-item checklist (medication management ownership, driving, isolation, own chronic conditions, missed visits) and refers them, with consent, to the program. After the death, a community health worker does a home visit within 72 hours, books a primary care appointment within 14 days, does a medication reconciliation, sets up meal delivery and transport, and runs structured check-ins at 2 weeks, 6 weeks and 6 months. The 6-week and 6-month checks include a prolonged grief screen (PG-13-R). Screen-positive people are referred to therapists trained in prolonged grief disorder treatment, billable to insurance because PGD has had its own diagnosis code (F43.81) since October 2022.
ideas.why_now: Medicare Advantage margins are under pressure, and plans are hunting for measurable avoidable-utilization programs and star-rating improvements. Value-based primary care and ACOs are expanding, and both are rewarded for preventing ED visits and admissions. Prolonged grief disorder became an official DSM-5-TR diagnosis in 2022, with an ICD-10-CM code from October 2022, so the treatment side is finally billable. Hospices are being asked to show quality beyond death itself. I could not verify current bereavement benefit designs at specific plans, so check that before pitching.
ideas.revenue_model: A per-enrolled-spouse fee of about $150 to $300 per month for 6 months, paid by the plan or ACO. This can convert to shared savings once there are a few hundred enrollees. Hospices receive a per-referral fee or a bereavement-outsourcing fee. Therapy referrals bill insurance directly, and the program can hold a small clinician panel. Employer benefit teams are a later channel.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The highest-risk patient is not on the payer's radar and is not the patient the hospice is paid to look after. Only the hospice team knows the caregiver is fading, and it knows months before any claim or enrollment record does. The widowhood effect (well documented in the research literature, with elevated mortality and hospitalization in the months after a spouse dies) is an underpriced, predictable utilization event.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one regional hospice and one value-based primary care group or small MA plan with a few thousand lives. Build the checklist and a simple spreadsheet workflow, then hire one community health worker or licensed social worker. Enroll the first 20 spouses at no charge, tracking ED visits, missed PCP visits and grief screens at 90 and 180 days. Use the data to sell a paid pilot to the plan or group before month 6. Get a HIPAA lawyer to sign off on the referral pathway and consent language.

ideas.title: DIC Finder for Veteran Families at Funerals
ideas.one_liner: A tool that reads a veteran's death certificate, hospice diagnosis and DD-214 to spot survivor benefits the widow does not know exist, sold to funeral homes and hospices rather than to families.
ideas.customer: Funeral homes (roughly 18,000 to 19,000 in the U.S.) that want a differentiated service for veteran families, and hospices with veteran programs. State veteran departments and accredited service officers are downstream partners.
ideas.problem: The Vietnam-era generation is now in the last phase of life and forms a large share of veteran deaths. The PACT Act (2022) expanded presumptive conditions for Agent Orange, burn pit and other exposures, so many widows may qualify for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC, on the order of $1,700 a month, check the current rate). Others may qualify for the Aid and Attendance survivor pension, or accrued benefits. Most never file. The death certificate says 'cardiac arrest' or 'respiratory failure' rather than the underlying service-connected condition. The funeral director's VA paperwork is only for the flag, headstone and burial allowance, and nobody reads the chart for exposure history. The hospice chaplain hears the veteran's service story at the bedside and the widow's money worries at the kitchen table, but has no tool to connect them.
ideas.solution: A web and mobile intake tool run at the arrangement conference or at the hospice bereavement visit. It photographs the DD-214, asks a 5-minute exposure and service history (deployment dates and locations, unit, conditions), and matches them against presumptive-condition and location lists. It flags likely DIC, survivor pension and accrued-benefit eligibility, and pre-fills VA Form 21P-534EZ. It then hands the case, with a warm introduction, to an accredited VSO representative or an accredited claims agent. The tool also stores the veteran's story fields so a funeral home can honor the person accurately.
ideas.why_now: The PACT Act has created a large wave of newly presumptive conditions, and claim volumes at the VA are at record levels. Vietnam-era veterans are aging into their peak mortality years. As I understand VA rules, accredited representatives can only charge fees after an initial decision, and legislation to tighten fees on predatory claim sharks has been moving. That pushes the sustainable model toward a B2B payer, not families. AI document extraction now makes DD-214 and death-certificate parsing cheap and reliable. Confirm current DIC rates and fee rules before launch.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS for funeral homes at $149 to $299 a month per location, with a per-case add-on for premium processing. Hospices and state veteran departments pay a per-completed-referral fee or a flat annual license. The VSO or accredited-agent partner pays for qualified leads only where the rules allow it, so this must be reviewed by counsel. Families pay nothing.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The money is unclaimed not because widows are lazy but because the trigger event is the funeral, and the only professional in the room (the funeral director) has no financial incentive or training to read a service history. Funeral homes will pay to look like heroes to veteran families, since it feeds pre-need referrals for the next generation, which is where their margin lives.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with one accredited county veteran service officer and two independent funeral homes near a large veteran population. Build the intake as a form plus a manual review by the VSO in week one, before any automation. Run 15 real cases at no charge and record dollars unlocked per family. Use those numbers to close five paying funeral homes at $149 a month. Have a veterans-law attorney review the fee and referral structure before charging anyone.

ideas.title: Two A.M. Any-Tradition Rites and Interpreter Line
ideas.one_liner: A 24/7 dispatch of vetted ritual specialists and death-trained interpreters for families outside the majority faith, sold to hospices and palliative units.
ideas.customer: Hospices, hospital palliative units and nursing homes in metros with large immigrant and non-Christian populations. They pay a monthly retainer plus per-dispatch fees.
ideas.problem: Most hospice chaplains are generalists trained in a Christian or interfaith pastoral model, and chaplain FTEs are among the first things cut when margins tighten. When an imam, Hindu priest, Buddhist monk, Sikh granthi, Hmong ritual specialist, Orthodox priest, or Native elder is needed, the family often gets the default chaplain, and the ritual windows are short and unforgiving. Some rites happen only before death, others require that the body not be moved or touched for hours, or that someone be present continuously. Standard hospice protocol says 'call the funeral home now.' Language is the second failure. Family members interpret for the patient and quietly soften bad news. In many languages the word 'dying' is unsayable. Interpreter contracts are priced per minute and built for clinic visits, with no death vocabulary or truth-telling norm training.
ideas.solution: A dispatch line and app for the hospice chaplain or on-call nurse. It connects to a vetted, paid roster of ritual specialists by tradition and language who can arrive or join by video, plus a small pool of interpreters who have completed a 40-hour end-of-life interpreting course (death vocabulary, family-filtering, cultural norms about naming prognosis). A one-page 'rite card' library is loaded into the hospice's EHR or intranet for each tradition. It gives the practical do's and don'ts: how to position the patient, what not to do to the body, who should not touch it, how long to wait before calling the funeral home, and what the family may ask for. Start with one metro and 4 to 6 traditions.
ideas.why_now: AI translation is tempting hospices to cut interpreter budgets, while civil-rights language-access rules (Section 1557 of the ACA as revised in 2024) push toward qualified interpreters and human review of machine translation for critical content. Confirm the current status of those rules. The older-adult population is more foreign-born and religiously diverse than a decade ago, and the unaffiliated 'nones' need secular rituals too. Chaplain staffing is shrinking. Consolidated hospice chains want scalable ways to meet 'emotional and spiritual support' quality measures.
ideas.revenue_model: A monthly retainer of $1,500 to $4,000 per hospice or hospital for 24/7 access. Per-dispatch fees ($150 to $300 to the specialist, with a 30 to 40 percent platform margin). Premium per-minute interpreting rates above standard telephone rates. Training and certification revenue from the interpreter course, sold to language-service companies and hospitals. Family fees are not charged.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not spiritual care in general but time-critical, tradition-specific competence at the exact hour of death, which a generalist chaplain honestly cannot supply. Family interpreters are the largest hidden source of bad-news distortion in end-of-life care. Whoever builds the roster and the interpreter standard owns a moat that AI translation cannot cross, because the value is trust and ritual authority, not words.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro where you know the communities (for example Minneapolis–St. Paul for Hmong, Somali and Karen families, or Houston or Queens for a wider mix). Recruit 20 to 25 ritual specialists and interpreters through mosque, temple and community boards, and pay them a small stipend for a 3-hour training on hospice basics. Build the rite-card library with their input. Sign two hospices to a free 60-day pilot on a shared phone number, then convert them to a retainer and use their case counts in a pitch to the next five.

ideas.title: Verbal-Promise Ledger for Mine Community Relations
ideas.one_liner: A voice-first, offline-capable phone tool that turns every promise a mine makes at community assemblies (Spanish, Quechua, Aymara) into a tracked commitment register the community can verify by WhatsApp.
ideas.customer: Heads of social performance and community relations at mid-tier copper and lithium operators and developers in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Bolivia. The second buyer is the E&S team at the lender or DFI (IFC, EXIM, DFC, export credit agencies). Budget is roughly $2-6k per month per project, charged to a risk or permitting line, not to IT.
ideas.problem: Insiders know that projects get blockaded over small, forgotten verbal promises, not over the headline issue. Examples are a promised well repair, a local-hire quota, or a dust-suppression schedule. The promise is made at a 2pm assembly and recorded on a paper acta, in a notebook, or in a WhatsApp voice note. Community-relations staff rotate every 12-24 months, contractors make their own promises, and nobody indexes the actas. Two years later the community says 'you promised' and shuts the road. The Las Bambas corridor closures, Jujuy lithium protests and Tia Maria all fit this pattern of trust debt. The mine cannot prove what it did or did not commit to, and neither can the community.
ideas.solution: Field officers record assemblies on a phone and snap a photo of the signed acta. Speech-to-text, tuned for Andean Spanish and human-checked for Quechua and Aymara, extracts discrete commitments: who promised what, to whom, and by when. Each one is assigned an internal owner and a due date. Community leaders get a receipt as a WhatsApp voice note or pictogram and can confirm, dispute, or mark it done. Ops managers and the CFO see 'commitment debt' aging, like a technical-debt dashboard. One-click exports meet IFC Performance Standard 1 and Equator Principles grievance and commitment register requirements. Community-side verification is the moat. It makes this a trust tool, not a surveillance tool.
ideas.why_now: Speech models are good enough for accented, code-switched Spanish, and usable for Quechua with a human in the loop. WhatsApp is universal in rural Andean communities. Lenders are demanding auditable social-license evidence for critical-mineral financings, including EU CRMA strategic projects and US DOE/DFC/EXIM deals. Argentina's RIGI regime is pulling lithium and copper projects into provinces with little consultation history. Peru and Chile have changed governments (2026), which reopens community negotiations. Staff turnover after the 2024-25 cost-cutting rounds has made institutional memory worse.
ideas.revenue_model: SaaS at $2-6k per month per project, plus a per-community onboarding fee ($1-3k). A one-off 'commitment debt audit' of historical actas is priced at $5-15k. Later, a lender-grade verified engagement score and a lender or insurer data licence.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Conflict risk is mostly commitment debt, meaning unanswered small promises lost through staff rotation, not big ideological opposition. Buyers think they need sentiment analysis. What they need is a receipt system. Giving the community the receipt is what makes the mine's data credible to lenders and inspectors.
ideas.first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, recruit two junior or mid-tier developers currently in a consultation round. Sell a $5-10k 'commitment debt audit': scan their last 12 months of actas and meeting minutes, and use an LLM plus a local linguist to extract every commitment and flag the overdue ones. This works with no integration, just PDFs and photos. The overdue list is usually shocking, and it converts to a SaaS pilot for the next assembly round. Use a WhatsApp Business API bot and an offline recorder app for v1. Do not build a custom platform yet.

ideas.title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
ideas.one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
ideas.customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
ideas.problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
ideas.solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
ideas.why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
