ideas.revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.

ideas.title: Orphan-Element Audits for Copper Concentrate and Tailings
ideas.one_liner: A 90-day survey that measures the tellurium, selenium, bismuth, cobalt, germanium, rhenium, indium and scandium copper mines already ship for free, then brokers by-product credit rights with refiners.
ideas.customer: Mid-size copper miners (Arizona, Utah, Nevada, Chile, Peru, Zambia, Kazakhstan) who sell concentrate to smelters or run SX-EW, paying $40-120k per site survey. Refiners and specialty-metal buyers (Aurubis-type smelters, Umicore, 5N Plus-type processors) pay finder fees. Government programmes such as DoD DPA Title III and DLA support recovery projects.
ideas.problem: Smelter contracts pay for Cu, Au and Ag. Te, Se, Bi, Co, Ge, In, Sb and Re are either given away, or shown only as penalty elements (As, Sb, Bi, Hg, F). The plant lab measures the penalty elements and stops. The 48-element ICP-MS suite exists only on exploration drill core from ten years ago and never on the concentrate, tailings, SX raffinate or electrolyte bleed streams. The smelter quietly captures value in anode slimes and flue dust. The miner has no data to negotiate with. Meanwhile, benchmark treatment charges for 2026 reportedly collapsed to around zero, so smelters are squeezed and newly hunting for by-product margin and for clean feed. Chinese export controls on Te, Bi, In, Ga, Ge, Sb and others make Western buyers desperate.
ideas.solution: A productised survey: pull 30-60 retained samples from process streams (every mine keeps monthly composite retains), run multi-element ICP-MS plus automated mineralogy through partner labs, and deliver an 'orphan-element balance' showing tonnes per year and contained value per element. Then hand the mine a negotiation kit: by-product participation clauses for offtake contracts, dust and slime credit language, and penalty-threshold renegotiation. Route the data to refiners and toll processors who can recover the element. The compensation is a survey fee plus 10-20% of by-product margin for 5 years, or a finder fee at contract signing.
ideas.why_now: In 2025 China imposed export controls on tellurium, bismuth, indium, gallium, germanium and antimony, with rare earths restrictions following. US and EU strategic stockpile, offtake and grant programmes now pay for domestic by-product supply. Smelters are under profit pressure from near-zero treatment charges and are open to sharing upside with suppliers. Prices for Te and Bi jumped.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-120k per site survey, plus a 10-20% by-product royalty or finder fee on recovered element revenue, plus a refiner-side subscription for a pipeline of quantified feed.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The barrier is not technology. Kennecott has produced tellurium for decades. It is that nobody measured, so nobody owns the value, and contracts were signed when no one cared. The person who knows how the process streams flow (where it goes to anode slimes, where to dust) can tell which stream concentrates each element.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask ten friendly mid-tier mines for retained composite samples, or buy access to public tailings and concentrate assays. Run 15 multi-element packs at $60-150 each (about $2k in total). Produce a one-page 'value at stake' per mine and email it to 30 operations and commercial managers. Sell 2-3 pilot surveys at $25k. Meanwhile call two refiners and one federal programme office with the resulting map to line up demand.

ideas.title: Real-Brine Library and DLE Benchmark Lab
ideas.one_liner: A neutral bank of characterised real brines, matrix-matched reference materials and public bake-offs of direct lithium extraction vendors, so nobody has to run a $3M private pilot to compare technologies.
ideas.customer: Three payers. First, brine developers (Smackover, Salton Sea geothermal, Argentine and Chilean salars, Utah and Nevada, Canadian oilfield brines) buying screening reports of $15-40k. Second, DLE vendors paying $30-80k per benchmark round for credible independent data. Third, commercial labs paying $2-3k per year for proficiency testing and buying CRMs.
ideas.problem: DLE vendors demonstrate on synthetic or 'friendly' brines. Real brines differ in Mg, Ca, Fe, Mn, silica, organics, H2S and temperature. Sorbent life, water balance and reagent cost only show up after hundreds of cycles, so every developer runs its own bespoke pilot ($1-5M, 12-18 months), and claims cannot be compared. On top of that, high-TDS brines (200-400 g/L) are notoriously hard to assay. Different labs disagree by 5-15% because of matrix effects, so 'recovery' computed from assay is shaky. Sealed drums of characterised brine from finished pilots sit unused in every developer's yard.
ideas.solution: Collect 12-20 characterised brines, anonymised if the owner wishes, stabilised in sealed drums. Run standardised bench protocols with vendors (50-100 sorption and desorption cycles, membrane or solvent equivalents) and publish scorecards on Li recovery, Mg and Ca rejection, water use, reagent cost per tonne LCE and degradation curve. Sell matrix-matched brine CRMs and inter-laboratory proficiency rounds to labs, and publish a certified-lab list. Developers buy cheap 'technology screening' reports that shortlist vendors before committing to a pilot. Lenders' independent engineers cite the benchmark.
ideas.why_now: After the 2023-25 lithium price collapse, investors will only fund bankable, independently verified technology. A wave of DLE technology-selection decisions is happening now in the Smackover, Argentina (RIGI-backed projects), Chile and geothermal brines. The vendor field is crowded and undifferentiated, so vendors will pay for third-party proof.
ideas.revenue_model: Vendor benchmark fees ($30-80k per brine set), developer report subscriptions ($15-40k per year), CRM sales, and proficiency-test scheme fees ($2-3k per lab per year), plus certification.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone thinks DLE is a chemistry problem. In practice it is a brine-specific reliability and data-credibility problem, and no one has standard reference brines, so every claim is unfalsifiable. The killers are minor components (silica, organics, Fe and Mn oxidation) that wreck sorbents after 200 cycles, which a fast pilot on an easy brine never shows. The insider knows that the leftover barrel is the asset.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask five friendly developers and labs for 20 L of retained brine (leftover after pilots). Characterise each with two labs. Invite three DLE vendors to co-fund a bake-off on one shared brine. Sell an inter-laboratory round to 6 labs at $2k each (about $12k in the first month) and pre-sell a $10k screening report to 3 developers. Publish the interlab bias chart as the marketing piece.

ideas.title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
ideas.one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
ideas.customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
ideas.problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
ideas.solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
ideas.why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
ideas.revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
ideas.first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.
